idiom_name: hand-written pthread pool over epoll_wait/select(2) with a mutex plus condition-variable leader token
implementation_notes: POSIX supplies only the pieces: pthread_create for the fixed pool, pthread_mutex_t/pthread_cond_t for the leader token and the waiting followers, and epoll_wait/kqueue/select for readiness. join() locks, waits while a leader exists, claims the leader slot, unlocks, blocks in the demultiplexer, then re-locks, clears the slot, signals a follower and processes the ready handle as the former leader. Two details decide correctness: the deactivate/reactivate protocol around the ready descriptor (remove it or run it one-shot before dispatch and rearm it afterwards, so the promoted leader cannot demultiplex the same event twice), and the fact that select(2)/poll(2) must not be called by several threads on one descriptor set - with epoll(7) the kernel hands an edge-triggered event to a single waiting thread, so several pool members may block in the same epoll_wait and the user-space promotion protocol becomes optional.
pitfalls: Calling select(2)/poll(2) from several threads on the same descriptor set produces duplicate readiness notifications; either serialise the pool or move to epoll/kqueue with a one-shot or edge-triggered mode that is rearmed after each dispatch.
Holding the pool mutex while blocked in epoll_wait/select freezes every follower; the leader must release the lock before waiting.
Forgetting to deactivate/rearm a ready descriptor before dispatching lets the promoted leader demultiplex the same event twice.
pthread_cond_signal restarts exactly one waiting thread but does not say which, so the promotion order is implementation-defined unless the pool keeps its own stack or priority queue.
Registering or deregistering descriptors from non-leader threads requires an explicit wakeup (eventfd or self-pipe) or the sleeping leader never sees the new interest set.
